title: How do you prevent one large customer from hurting everyone else when your system is multi-tenant at the application layer but shares infrastructure — and why is "just add more instances" insufficient when the bottleneck is a shared database, a third-party API quota, or a single Kafka partition?
shortTitle: How do you stop one large customer hurting everyone when infrastructure is shared?

s1_definition.profdef: When a system runs many stateless application instances but those instances all converge on a shared bottleneck — a single database, a third-party API with a fixed quota, or a single Kafka partition for a key — then one large customer can saturate that shared bottleneck and degrade every tenant, regardless of how many application instances exist. Adding more application instances does not help because the scarce resource is downstream of the instances: more instances simply means more clients hammering the same database connection limit, the same external quota, or the same partition's single-consumer ordering. The fix must act at the point of contention: per-tenant fairness and concurrency limits on the shared resource, partitioning or sharding so one customer's load lands on isolated capacity, a shared connection proxy that caps and fairly allocates connections, per-tenant quotas against external APIs, and spreading hot keys across more partitions. Scaling the stateless layer is only useful when the bottleneck is actually the stateless layer.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India can hire as many tellers as it likes, but if every transaction has to be stamped by the one manager who holds the only key to the vault, then hiring a hundred more tellers just means a hundred more people queued at the one manager's door. If a giant corporate client sends ten thousand transactions, the manager is swamped and Rajesh's simple withdrawal waits behind them — and more tellers do nothing because the manager is the bottleneck, not the tellers. The bank must fix the real constraint: give the manager a rule that no single client may occupy more than a fair share of their time, or appoint several managers each responsible for a different set of accounts so one client's flood only occupies one manager. Adding tellers is the wrong lever when the manager is the chokepoint.
s1_definition.oneliner: More application instances cannot relieve a shared downstream bottleneck — fix it at the point of contention with per-tenant fairness, sharding, a connection proxy, external quotas, and hot-key spreading.

The fix must act at the point of contention: per-tenant fairness and concurrency limits on the shared resource, partitioning or sharding so one customer's load lands on isolated capacity, a shared connection proxy that caps and fairly allocates connections, per-tenant quotas against external APIs, and spreading hot keys across more partitions. Scaling the stateless layer is only useful when the bottleneck is actually the stateless layer.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India can hire as many tellers as it likes, but if every transaction has to be stamped by the one manager who holds the only key to the vault, then hiring a hundred more tellers just means a hundred more people queued at the one manager's door. If a giant corporate client sends ten thousand transactions, the manager is swamped and Rajesh's simple withdrawal waits behind them — and more tellers do nothing because the manager is the bottleneck, not the tellers. **One line to remember:** More application instances cannot relieve a shared downstream bottleneck — fix it at the point of contention with per-tenant fairness, sharding, a connection proxy, external quotas, and hot-key spreading.

sections.s3_banking:
At National Bank of India, the payments service runs many stateless instances behind a load balancer, but all instances share one database connection pool, one third-party gateway quota, and a Kafka topic partitioned by customer id. A large corporate customer, BigCorp, sends a flood of transfers.

Problem 1 — the shared database. BigCorp's heavy queries consume the shared connections, and Rajesh's simple balance check waits. The operations team tries adding five more instances, and it gets worse, because the extra instances open even more connections and exhaust the database's connection limit.

Problem 2 — the shared gateway quota. BigCorp's flood burns the whole thousand-per-second gateway budget, so the provider throttles the bank entirely and every tenant's payments fail.

Problem 3 — the single Kafka partition. Because the partition key is the customer id, all of BigCorp's events land on one partition consumed by one consumer, so they back up and add latency, and adding consumers does nothing.

The fix demonstrates diagnosing low instance CPU with high latency, then applying the point-of-contention remedies: a bounded shared connection proxy with per-tenant query concurrency, a per-tenant sub-quota on the gateway, and a composite partition key that spreads BigCorp across partitions. The mini-project builds a `SharedBottleneck` simulator for each of the three, shows that adding instances does not help, and shows the correct fix bounding BigCorp while protecting other tenants.
sections.s5_journey:
Input: BigCorp floods the shared database, the shared gateway quota, and a single Kafka partition, while Rajesh and Priya make ordinary requests. The team has already observed that instance CPU is low while latency is high, pointing downstream.

Step 1 — Shared database. BigCorp fires eight queries. The per-tenant concurrency cap of five accepts five and rejects three with a per-tenant warning, so BigCorp cannot hold more than five of the shared connections. Rajesh's single balance query then acquires a connection immediately because BigCorp was bounded. Adding instances would not have helped, because the real connection cap of fifty is shared regardless.

Step 2 — Shared gateway quota. BigCorp makes five gateway calls, but its sub-quota is three, so three succeed and two are rejected with a quota warning. The remaining shared budget is preserved, so Priya's gateway call succeeds. Without per-tenant sub-quotas, BigCorp could have burned the whole budget and the provider would have throttled everyone.

Step 3 — Hot Kafka partition. Using the customer-id key, all six of BigCorp's accounts hash to a single partition — the hot-key set has size one — so all load lands on one consumer and backs up. Using the composite customer-plus-account key, the six accounts spread across multiple partitions, so the load parallelises across consumers.

Step 4 — Diagnosis confirmed. In every case the bottleneck was a shared downstream resource, not the stateless instances, which is why low instance CPU coexisted with high latency. The correct remedies acted at the point of contention.

Step 5 — Outcome. BigCorp was contained at the database, the gateway, and the partition level, and Rajesh and Priya were protected — all without adding a single application instance.

sections.s6_takeaway:
The key realisation is that a system can be fully horizontally scaled at the stateless application layer and still be brought to its knees by one large customer, because the real bottleneck is often a resource shared across all those instances rather than the instances themselves. When that is the case, adding more instances is not neutral — it is harmful, because every new instance is another client competing for the same scarce downstream resource. So the first thing I do is diagnose which resource is actually saturated, and the classic tell is that instance CPU and memory are low while latency is high and errors are concentrated, which means the instances are sitting idle waiting on something shared beneath them.

There are three shared bottlenecks I would call out specifically. The first is a shared database: it has a finite connection limit and finite I/O, and adding instances only opens more connections and can exhaust the limit faster. The fix is a connection proxy like PgBouncer that multiplexes a bounded number of real connections no matter how many instances exist, per-tenant query concurrency so one customer cannot hold all the connections, read replicas to offload heavy readers, and ultimately sharding so the largest customer lives on its own shard. The second is a third-party API quota: if the provider allows a fixed number of calls per second across the whole account, adding instances just means more of them racing to burn it, and one big customer can consume it all and get everyone throttled. The fix is a shared distributed rate limiter enforcing per-tenant sub-quotas so each tenant gets a fair slice.

The third is a single Kafka partition. Kafka orders within a partition, and a partition is read by exactly one consumer in a group, so if the partition key is the customer id, all of a large customer's events land on one partition and one consumer, and adding consumers does nothing because the extras sit idle — a partition cannot be split. The fix is to increase partition count and choose a key that spreads the customer's load across many partitions, for example a composite of customer and account, while preserving ordering only at the grain that genuinely needs it.

In my banking work this came up when a large corporate customer's flood degraded everyone and the first instinct — add five more instances — made it worse by exhausting the database connection limit. The fix was to act at the point of contention: a bounded shared connection proxy with per-tenant query concurrency, a per-tenant sub-quota against the payment gateway, and a composite partition key that spread the customer across the topic. The principle I carry into interviews is that horizontal scaling of the stateless tier solves exactly one kind of bottleneck, and using it against a shared database, a shared external quota, or a hot partition is both a waste of money and a way to deepen the outage. Fairness and isolation have to live where the contention actually is.
